- Current health concerns and risk factors:  4–5-day flare of chronic atopic dermatitis—diffuse erythematous, very pruritic, dry skin on chest, hands, arms; worst in antecubital fossae. History of asthma (intermittent, uses blue inhaler PRN).

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Widespread, non-weepy, intensely pruritic erythematous dermatitis in patient with known eczema; no systemic symptoms; poor response to current emollient and low-potency steroid.  

Working diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare—high likelihood (consistent with chronic history and classic flexural distribution).  

Differential diagnoses:  
• Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis—moderate likelihood given acute worsening though no new exposures reported.  
• Scabies infestation—low likelihood; pruritus present but no burrows or contact history.  

Management priorities: Reduce inflammation/pruritus, escalate topical steroid potency, initiate non-sedating antihistamine, continue regular emollient use, monitor response within 2 weeks.  

Management Plan

- Prescribed Fexofenadine (oral antihistamine) and Betnovate cream twice daily for 2 weeks.  
- Continue Diprobase emollient cream and Dermol shower wash.  
- Continue PRN salbutamol inhaler for asthma as needed.  
- Educated patient on fingertip-unit amounts of topical steroid and to apply thinly.  
- Advised to return sooner if worsening or adverse reaction; otherwise review after 2 weeks.  
- Prescription sent electronically to patient’s nominated Boots pharmacy.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Follow-up for eczema flare in 2 weeks; other preventive care not recorded  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare – High likelihood: chronic condition with classic distribution and symptoms; exacerbation described.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood: acute severe worsening could reflect new exposure; less favored as patient reports no changes.  
3. Scabies infestation – Low likelihood: intense itch and flexural involvement but absence of burrows, nocturnal predominance, or contact history.

● Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (BP, pulse), BMI/anthropometrics, smoking/alcohol history, dietary and exercise assessment, immunisation review, mental health screening, routine preventive screening (cervical, STI, metabolic bloods).  
● Internal contradictions: Family history—patient states mother has hypothyroidism; clinician repeats “hyperthyroidism” (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; some minor interruptions and incomplete phrases but clinical information understandable.
